claim: Optical tweezers use tightly focused laser beams to trap silica or polystyrene beads in a harmonic potential.
source: OTs use tightly focused laser beams to trap silica or polystyrene beads in a harmonic potential (Zhang et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established principle of optical tweezers supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: High-resolution optical tweezers achieve spatiotemporal resolution of approximately 0.3 nm and 20 µs.
source: High-resolution OTs achieve extremely high spatiotemporal resolution (~0.3 nm, ~20 µs) in a range of force that can reversibly unfold a biomolecule or is generated by molecular motors (Abbondanzieri et al., 2005; Neupane et al., 2016; Moffitt et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2012; Cecconi et al., 2005; Bustamante et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Optical tweezers can apply forces in the range of 0.02–250 pN to single molecules.
source: The beads act as force and displacement sensors while applying tiny forces (0.02–250 pN) to single molecules attached to the beads.
evidence: This is a stated capability of the optical tweezers system, supported by citation context.

claim: C2 domains from E-Syt2 and Syt1 resisted unbinding forces of 2–7 pN.
source: C2 domains from either protein resisted unbinding forces of 2–7 pN and had binding energies of 4–14 kBT per C2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: C2 domains from E-Syt2 and Syt1 had binding energies of 4–14 kBT per C2 domain.
source: C2 domains from either protein resisted unbinding forces of 2–7 pN and had binding energies of 4–14 kBT per C2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements in Table 1.

claim: E-Syt2 C2AB has a binding energy of 4.6 kBT with membrane tether in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: With membranes composed of 85% POPC, 10% DOPS and 5% PI(4,5)P2, we obtained binding energies of 4.6 kBT for E-Syt2 C2AB, 7.4 kBT for Syt1 C2B, 10.8 kBT for Syt1 C2AB (all in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+), and of 12 kBT for E-Syt2 C2C in zero Ca2+.
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: Syt1 C2B has a binding energy of 7.4 kBT with membrane tether in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: With membranes composed of 85% POPC, 10% DOPS and 5% PI(4,5)P2, we obtained binding energies of 4.6 kBT for E-Syt2 C2AB, 7.4 kBT for Syt1 C2B, 10.8 kBT for Syt1 C2AB (all in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+), and of 12 kBT for E-Syt2 C2C in zero Ca2+.
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: Syt1 C2AB has a binding energy of 10.8 kBT with membrane tether in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: With membranes composed of 85% POPC, 10% DOPS and 5% PI(4,5)P2, we obtained binding energies of 4.6 kBT for E-Syt2 C2AB, 7.4 kBT for Syt1 C2B, 10.8 kBT for Syt1 C2AB (all in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+), and of 12 kBT for E-Syt2 C2C in zero Ca2+.
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: E-Syt2 C2C has a binding energy of 12 kBT with membrane tether in zero Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: With membranes composed of 85% POPC, 10% DOPS and 5% PI(4,5)P2, we obtained binding energies of 4.6 kBT for E-Syt2 C2AB, 7.4 kBT for Syt1 C2B, 10.8 kBT for Syt1 C2AB (all in the presence of 100 μM Ca2+), and of 12 kBT for E-Syt2 C2C in zero Ca2+.
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The equilibrium force for E-Syt2 C2AB is 2.9 pN under conditions of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: The corresponding equilibrium forces, i.e. the forces at which the unbinding probability is 0.5, increase in the same order (2.9 pN, 3.1 pN, 4.7 pN, and 6.5 pN).
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The equilibrium force for Syt1 C2B is 3.1 pN under conditions of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: The corresponding equilibrium forces, i.e. the forces at which the unbinding probability is 0.5, increase in the same order (2.9 pN, 3.1 pN, 4.7 pN, and 6.5 pN).
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The equilibrium force for Syt1 C2AB is 4.7 pN under conditions of 100 μM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: The corresponding equilibrium forces, i.e. the forces at which the unbinding probability is 0.5, increase in the same order (2.9 pN, 3.1 pN, 4.7 pN, and 6.5 pN).
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The equilibrium force for E-Syt2 C2C is 6.5 pN under conditions of zero Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: The corresponding equilibrium forces, i.e. the forces at which the unbinding probability is 0.5, increase in the same order (2.9 pN, 3.1 pN, 4.7 pN, and 6.5 pN).
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) is 1.0 (±0.3) nm for E-Syt2 C2AB.
source: We estimated the distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) to be 1.0 (±0.3, standard deviation) nm for E-Syt2 C2AB, 1.4 (±0.5) nm for Syt1 C2AB, and 0.7 (±0.2) nm for E-Syt2 C2C (see Materials and Methods) (Bustamante et al., 2004; Rebane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data using established models.

claim: The distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) is 1.4 (±0.5) nm for Syt1 C2AB.
source: We estimated the distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) to be 1.0 (±0.3, standard deviation) nm for E-Syt2 C2AB, 1.4 (±0.5) nm for Syt1 C2AB, and 0.7 (±0.2) nm for E-Syt2 C2C (see Materials and Methods) (Bustamante et al., 2004; Rebane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data using established models.

claim: The distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) is 0.7 (±0.2) nm for E-Syt2 C2C.
source: We estimated the distance between the transition state and the bound state (Δx‡) to be 1.0 (±0.3, standard deviation) nm for E-Syt2 C2AB, 1.4 (±0.5) nm for Syt1 C2AB, and 0.7 (±0.2) nm for E-Syt2 C2C (see Materials and Methods) (Bustamante et al., 2004; Rebane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data using established models.

claim: E-Syt2 C2AB membrane binding is Ca2+-dependent.
source: We have also observed that, in contrast, membrane binding by E-Syt2 C2AB depends on Ca2+, again in agreement with other reports (Min et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations.

claim: E-Syt2 C2C binds to membranes in a PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
source: For E-Syt2, we found that its C2C domain binds to membranes strongly in a PI(4,5)P2-dependent, but calcium-independent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments and consistent with previous observations in cells.

claim: E-Syt2 C2C binds to membranes in a calcium-independent manner.
source: For E-Syt2, we found that its C2C domain binds to membranes strongly in a PI(4,5)P2-dependent, but calcium-independent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 2D and consistent with previous observations.

claim: Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Recapitulating previous reports (Min et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015; Giordano et al., 2013), we found that Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a Ca2+-, DOPS-, and PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a DOPS-dependent manner.
source: Recapitulating previous reports (Min et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015; Giordano et al., 2013), we found that Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a Ca2+-, DOPS-, and PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5B and supported by citations.

claim: Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
source: Recapitulating previous reports (Min et al., 2007; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015; Giordano et al., 2013), we found that Syt1 C2AB binds to membranes in a Ca2+-, DOPS-, and PI(4,5)P2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5B and supported by citations.

claim: The C2A and C2B domains of E-Syt2 strongly associate with each other to form a V-shaped structure.
source: The C2A and C2B domains of E-Syt2 strongly associate with each other to form a V-shaped structure (Figure 1A) and have not been purified separately (Schauder et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and is consistent with the observed reversible dissociation at 8-13 pN.

claim: At 12–22 pN force, the C2A domains of E-Syt2 and Syt1 undergo irreversible unfolding.
source: As the force was further increased, for both E-Syt2 C2AB and Syt1 C2AB two larger rips appeared in distinct force ranges, one at 12–22 pN (Figure 1C, green arrows), the other at 18–45 pN (cyan arrows) (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is observed in the force-extension curves and confirmed by experiments with individual domains.

claim: At 18–45 pN force, the C2B domains of E-Syt2 and Syt1 undergo irreversible unfolding.
source: As the force was further increased, for both E-Syt2 C2AB and Syt1 C2AB two larger rips appeared in distinct force ranges, one at 12–22 pN (Figure 1C, green arrows), the other at 18–45 pN (cyan arrows) (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is observed in the force-extension curves and confirmed by experiments with individual domains.

claim: The two Syt1 C2 domains bind to and unbind from membranes simultaneously within instrumental resolution.
source: Interestingly, although Syt1 C2A and C2B domains barely associate (Zhou et al., 2017) as they do in E-Syt2, the two Syt1 C2 domains bound to and unbound from membranes simultaneously within our instrumental resolution, as is indicated by the two-state transition (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in the extension-time trajectories showing two-state transitions.

claim: Syt1 C2B dominates membrane binding compared to C2A.
source: Hence, the two Syt1 C2 domains bind to membranes cooperatively, but the C2B dominates membrane binding, consistent with previous reports (Bai et al., 2004; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Voleti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing C2A barely binds while C2B binds at reduced force compared to C2AB, and is supported by citations.

claim: Reducing DOPS concentration from 20% to 10% decreased the binding equilibrium force of E-Syt2 C2AB from 3.6 pN to 2.9 pN.
source: Reducing the DOPS concentration from 20% to 10% decreased the binding equilibrium force of E-Syt2 C2AB from 3.6 pN to 2.9 pN and the binding energy from 7 kBT to 4.6 kBT (Table 1 and Figure 5A, top trace).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: Reducing DOPS concentration from 20% to 10% decreased the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2AB from 7 kBT to 4.6 kBT.
source: Reducing the DOPS concentration from 20% to 10% decreased the binding equilibrium force of E-Syt2 C2AB from 3.6 pN to 2.9 pN and the binding energy from 7 kBT to 4.6 kBT (Table 1 and Figure 5A, top trace).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Table 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: Reducing PI(4,5)P2 concentration from 5% to 2.5% decreased the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2C from ~12 kBT to ~10 kBT.
source: Similarly, reducing the PI(4,5)P2 concentration from 5% to 2.5% decreased the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2C from ~12 kBT to ~10 kBT and of Syt1 C2AB from ~10.8 kBT to ~7.8 kBT (Table 1, Figure 5B, top trace, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: Reducing PI(4,5)P2 concentration from 5% to 2.5% decreased the binding energy of Syt1 C2AB from ~10.8 kBT to ~7.8 kBT.
source: Similarly, reducing the PI(4,5)P2 concentration from 5% to 2.5% decreased the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2C from ~12 kBT to ~10 kBT and of Syt1 C2AB from ~10.8 kBT to ~7.8 kBT (Table 1, Figure 5B, top trace, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured effect shown in Table 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: Omitting PI(4,5)P2 minimized membrane binding of E-Syt2 C2AB in the presence of up to 30% DOPS.
source: Omitting PI(4,5)P2 minimized membrane binding of E-Syt2 C2AB in the presence of up to 30% DOPS (Figure 5A, middle trace) and of Syt1 C2AB in the presence of 10% DOPS (Figure 5B, middle trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Omitting PI(4,5)P2 minimized membrane binding of Syt1 C2AB in the presence of 10% DOPS.
source: Omitting PI(4,5)P2 minimized membrane binding of E-Syt2 C2AB in the presence of up to 30% DOPS (Figure 5A, middle trace) and of Syt1 C2AB in the presence of 10% DOPS (Figure 5B, middle trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increasing DOPS concentration to 40% for E-Syt2 C2AB at least partially rescued membrane binding in the absence of PI(4,5)P2.
source: However, increasing the DOPS concentration to 40% for E-Syt2 C2AB (Figure 5A, bottom trace) and 30% for Syt1 C2AB (Figure 5B, bottom trace) at least partially rescued their membrane binding in the absence of PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing DOPS concentration to 30% for Syt1 C2AB at least partially rescued membrane binding in the absence of PI(4,5)P2.
source: However, increasing the DOPS concentration to 40% for E-Syt2 C2AB (Figure 5A, bottom trace) and 30% for Syt1 C2AB (Figure 5B, bottom trace) at least partially rescued their membrane binding in the absence of PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Syt1 C2AB tightly bound to membrane containing 30% DOPS but no PI(4,5)P2 with a binding energy of 8.7 kBT.
source: In particular, Syt1 C2AB tightly bound to the membrane containing 30% DOPS but no PI(4,5)P2 with a binding energy of 8.7 kBT (Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured value shown in Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: As Ca2+ concentration increases, the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2AB quickly increases in 50–100 µM Ca2+, then plateaus around 100–200 µM Ca2+, and further increases in 200–500 µM Ca2+.
source: As the Ca2+ concentration increases, the binding energy of E-Syt2 C2AB quickly increases in 50–100 µM Ca2+, then plateaus around 100–200 µM Ca2+, and further increases in 200–500 µM Ca2+.
evidence: This is observed in the Ca2+-dependent measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: As NaCl concentration increased, the C2 domain-membrane affinity monotonically decreased.
source: As NaCl concentration increased, the C2 domain-membrane affinity monotonically decreased.
evidence: This is observed in the NaCl-dependent measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NaCl at high concentrations shields the electrostatic attractions between C2 and anionic lipids.
source: Thus, NaCl at high concentrations shields the electrostatic attractions between C2 and anionic lipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed decrease in affinity with increasing NaCl concentration and is consistent with known electrostatic effects.

claim: The forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are in the range of 2 to 7 pN.
source: For both E-Syt2 and Syt1, we have found that the forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are in the range of 2 to 7 pN, comparable to the forces generated by many motor proteins such as kinesin and myosin (Zhang et al., 2013), but are much lower, for example, than the forces produced by neuronal SNARE zippering (~17 pN) (Ma et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is derived from the equilibrium force measurements and compared to known forces from other systems.

claim: The forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are comparable to the forces generated by motor proteins such as kinesin and myosin.
source: For both E-Syt2 and Syt1, we have found that the forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are in the range of 2 to 7 pN, comparable to the forces generated by many motor proteins such as kinesin and myosin (Zhang et al., 2013), but are much lower, for example, than the forces produced by neuronal SNARE zippering (~17 pN) (Ma et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made based on measured forces and cited literature values.

claim: The forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are much lower than the forces produced by neuronal SNARE zippering (~17 pN).
source: For both E-Syt2 and Syt1, we have found that the forces generated by C2 domain binding to membranes are in the range of 2 to 7 pN, comparable to the forces generated by many motor proteins such as kinesin and myosin (Zhang et al., 2013), but are much lower, for example, than the forces produced by neuronal SNARE zippering (~17 pN) (Ma et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made based on measured forces and cited literature values.

claim: The unbinding rate is less sensitive to force than the binding rate for C2 domains.
source: Interestingly, the unbinding rate is less sensitive to force than the binding rate, as is indicated by the smaller slope of the logarithm of the unbinding rate than the slope for the binding rate.
evidence: This is observed in the force-dependent rate measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The bound C2 states are tightly confined near membrane surfaces.
source: This difference suggests that the bound C2 states are tightly confined near membrane surfaces (Bustamante et al., 2004; Rebane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the force-dependent rate measurements and supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: The positions of the transition states for unbinding are close to those of the bound states.
source: In other words, the positions of the transition states for unbinding are close to those of the bound states.
evidence: This is inferred from the short Δx‡ values measured for the C2 domains.

claim: Single or double C2 domains bind to membranes with lifetimes shorter than three seconds at zero force.
source: Our study shows that for both E-Syt2 and Syt1, single or double C2 domains bind to membranes with lifetimes shorter than three seconds at zero force and with even shorter lifetimes in the presence of external forces.
evidence: This is calculated from the unbinding rates at zero force shown in Table 1.

claim: The measured binding affinity, binding and unbinding rates of Syt1 C2AB in the presence of 100 µM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2 matched well with previous measurements under similar experimental conditions.
source: Our measured binding affinity, binding and unbinding rates in the presence of 100 µM Ca2+, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2 matched well previous measurements under similar experimental conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous work, with specific values given in the text.

claim: The corrected binding energy, binding rate, and unbinding rate of Syt1 C2AB are 12.8 kBT, 2.9 × 10^5 M^−1s^−1, and 1 s^−1, respectively.
source: The corrected binding energy, binding rate, and unbinding rate of Syt1 C2AB measured by us are consistent with the corresponding values recently reported (12.8 vs 13 kBT, 2.9 × 105 vs 4 × 105 M−1s−1, and 1 vs 1 s−1) (Pérez-Lara et al., 2016).
evidence: These are calculated values from the experimental data, shown to be consistent with cited literature.

claim: The membrane-binding energy for Syt1 C2A domain is estimated to be 3.8 (±0.9) kBT under conditions of 100 μM Ca2+, 200 mM NaCl, 85% POPC, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
source: Using the derived binding energies of the C2AB and C2B domains in the absence of membrane tethering, we estimated a membrane-binding energy for Syt1 C2A domain to be 3.8 (±0.9) kBT under the condition of 100 μM Ca2+, 200 mM NaCl, 85% POPC, 10% DOPS, and 5% PI(4,5)P2.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured binding energies of C2AB and C2B using a theoretical model.

claim: E-Syt2 C2A binds up to four Ca2+ with dissociation constants ranging from µM to >10 mM.
source: Whereas E-Syt2 C2B does not bind Ca2+, the C2A binds up to four Ca2+ with dissociation constants ranging from µM to >10 mM (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2014.

claim: E-Syt2 C2B does not bind Ca2+.
source: Whereas E-Syt2 C2B does not bind Ca2+, the C2A binds up to four Ca2+ with dissociation constants ranging from µM to >10 mM (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2014.

claim: The multiple-phase binding of C2 domains is consistent with the multi-valent Ca2+ binding by E-Syt2 C2AB and Syt1 C2AB.
source: The multiple-phase binding of C2 domains observed by us is consistent with the multi-valent Ca2+ binding by E-Syt2 C2AB and Syt1 C2AB (Xu et al., 2014; Chapman, 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed multi-phase Ca2+-dependent binding and supported by citations.

claim: Lipids in the supported bilayer are mobile, uniformly distributed around the bead surface, and free of visible defects.
source: Lipids in the supported bilayer are mobile, uniformly distributed around the bead surface, and free of visible defects, as reported previously (Baksh et al., 2004; Brouwer et al., 2015) (Figure 1A, inset, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence imaging and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The temperature decrease from 37°C to room temperature reduces the area per lipid in the bilayer.
source: The temperature decrease reduces the area per lipid in the bilayer (Petrache et al., 2000), which removes the possible excess membrane on the bead surface.
evidence: This is a known effect of temperature on lipid bilayers, supported by citation.

claim: The membranes are firmly attached to the silica surfaces in the force range of interest (<35 pN).
source: The continuous FEC regions corresponding to the same states in the presence and absence of supported bilayers for all three C2 domains generally overlapped (Figure 1C), indicating that the membranes are firmly attached to the silica surfaces and barely contribute to the measured extensions in the force range of interest (<35 pN).
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping FECs in the presence and absence of bilayers.

claim: The FECs are noisier in the presence of membranes than in their absence, possibly due to lateral diffusion of the lipids.
source: However, the FECs appear thicker and are thus noisier in the presence of membranes than in their absence (Figure 1C, compare black and blue FECs), possibly due to lateral diffusion of the lipids to which the C2 domains were attached (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the FECs and a possible explanation is provided based on lipid mobility.

claim: At 8–13 pN force, a small and often reversible jump occurred with E-Syt2 C2AB, likely representing dissociation of the two C2 domains.
source: At higher forces 8–13 pN, a small and often reversible jump occurred with E-Syt2 C2AB (Figure 1C, region in the first FEC marked by magenta dashed rectangle, and inset). This jump likely represents dissociation of the two C2 domains in the C2AB fragment of E-Syt2 (Figure 1D, transition between states 2 and 3 for E-Syt2 C2AB), as the C2A and C2B domains are bound to each other by a stable interface (Xu et al., 2014; Schauder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is observed in the FECs and interpreted based on structural knowledge from citations.

claim: The C2 domain is one of the most abundant and highly conserved membrane-binding modules, with ~200 C2 domains encoded by the human genome.
source: The C2 domain is one of the most abundant and highly conserved membrane-binding modules, with ~200 C2 domains encoded by the human genome (Lemmon, 2008; Corbalan-Garcia and Gómez-Fernández, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C2 domain binding to membranes is regulated by the phospholipid composition of the bilayer and in many cases is Ca2+-dependent.
source: Their binding to membranes is regulated by the phospholipid composition of the bilayer and in many cases is Ca2+-dependent (Südhof, 2013; Monteiro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Synaptotagmins act as Ca2+ sensors that cooperate with SNAREs to mediate Ca2+-triggered exocytosis.
source: They act as Ca2+ sensors that cooperate with soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment receptors (SNAREs) to mediate Ca2+-triggered exocytosis, leading to release of neurotransmitters, peptide hormones and a variety of other molecules (Südhof and Rothman, 2009; Zhou et al., 2017; Chapman, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Synaptotagmin function supported by citations.

claim: E-Syts are located on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and contain five (for E-Syt1) or three (for E-Syt2 and E-Syt3) C2 domains in addition to the SMP domain.
source: Different from Syts, E-Syts are located on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and contain five (for E-Syt1) or three (for E-Syt2 and E-Syt3) C2 domains in addition to the SMP domain (Min et al., 2007; Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about E-Syt structure supported by citations.

claim: E-Syt C2 domains regulate lipid transfer between the endoplasmic reticulum and the plasma membrane via the SMP domain.
source: E-Syt C2 domains regulate lipid transfer, instead of membrane fusion, between the endoplasmic reticulum and the plasma membrane via the SMP domain (Giordano et al., 2013; Saheki et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2016; Schauder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about E-Syt function supported by citations.

claim: Both Syts and E-Syts bind membranes in trans through their multiple C2 domains and are well-positioned to generate force to draw two membranes into proximity.
source: Therefore, both Syts and E-Syts bind membranes in trans through their multiple C2 domains and are well-positioned to generate force to draw two membranes into proximity required for membrane fusion or lipid exchange (van den Bogaart et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Krishnakumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional properties of these proteins and supported by citations.

claim: Constitutive ER-plasma membrane contacts mediated by E-Syt2 depend upon the Ca2+-independent binding of E-Syt2 C2C to PI(4,5)P2 in the plasma membrane.
source: This is consistent with observations in intact and semi-intact cells showing that constitutive ER-plasma membrane contacts mediated by E-Syt2 depend upon the Ca2+-independent binding of E-Syt2 C2C to PI(4,5)P2 in the plasma membrane (Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015; Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cell biology studies.

claim: Ca2+-dependent interaction of E-Syt2 C2AB with the membrane may relieve an autoinhibitory intramolecular interaction between C2AB and the SMP domain that prevents E-Syt2 from transferring lipids.
source: As suggested by results of a recent study, Ca2+-dependent interaction of E-Syt2 C2AB with the membrane may relieve an autoinhibitory intramolecular interaction between C2AB and the SMP domain (the lipid transport module of E-Syt2) that prevents E-Syt2 from transferring lipids (Xin Bian and Pietro De Camilli, unpublished results).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on unpublished results.

claim: Long-lived docking of membranes by Syt1 or E-Syts is a consequence of cooperativity among multiple molecules.
source: Nevertheless, membrane contacts observed in cells are mediated by multiple Syt1 and E-Syts, which may dimerize or oligomerize (Wang et al., 2014; Schauder et al., 2014; Giordano et al., 2013), as well as by additional proteins. Thus, long-lived docking of membranes by Syt1 or E-Syts is a consequence of cooperativity among multiple molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the short lifetimes of single domains and the known presence of multiple proteins in cellular contexts, supported by citations.

claim: An extremely high force of ~425 pN is required to pull apart a single membrane contact site between chloroplast and endoplasmic reticulum.
source: In support of this idea, an extremely high force of ~425 pN is required to pull apart a single membrane contact site between chloroplast and endoplasmic reticulum (Andersson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersson et al., 2007.

claim: The optical tweezers method can be widely applied to study protein–membrane interactions.
source: The method can be widely applied to study protein–membrane interactions.
